The body uses traditional Japanese woods such as hinoki cypress, pine or camphor, hollowed inside to resonate. The two heads are usually cowhide or horsehide, specially treated to make them durable and to improve the sound. The rim is reinforced with a wooden or metal hoop. The sticks (bachi) are of bamboo or wood, and the tip can be wrapped in cloth to change the tone.

Taiko is the general Japanese term for drums and percussion instruments, classified as membranophones, Hornbostel–Sachs 21. Its construction comes down to a body and heads, the common forms being the barrel-shaped nagado-daiko and the smaller shime-daiko, struck on the head with sticks. Besides being played singly, ensembles of different drums have developed, called kumidaiko. It is used at festivals, in the theatre, in gagaku, in kagura, in Buddhist rites, in the military and in concerts; besides Japanese groups, performers are found in the United States, Australia, Canada, Europe, Taiwan and Brazil.
和太鼓為日本膜鳴打擊樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號21。其起源有日本: Taiko is a Japanese membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 21. Its origins are the stuff of Japanese myth, while the historical record shows it arriving by the sixth century at the latest through Chinese and Korean cultural influence; haniwa figurines of the Kofun period already show drumming, and some forms resemble Indian instruments. Historically it has been used for communication, in the military, as theatre accompaniment, in religious rites and in concerts, and today it also takes part in the social movements of minority groups. In 1951 Daihachi Oguchi developed kumidaiko ensemble playing, and in 1961 groups such as Ondekoza made it popular, and it spread to the United States, Australia, Canada, Europe, Taiwan and Brazil.
和太鼓為日本膜鳴樂器，見於雅樂、能樂、歌舞伎、神樂、盂蘭盆節等傳統場合，也用於通: Taiko is a Japanese membranophone, heard on traditional occasions such as gagaku, noh, kabuki, kagura and obon, and also used for communication, in the military, in concerts and in the social movements of minority groups. A modern kumidaiko ensemble is built around barrel-shaped nagado drums of different sizes and smaller drums, and some groups add voices, strings and winds; certain scenes of the kabuki play The Tale of Shiroishi and the Taihei Chronicles are also accompanied by taiko.
和太鼓為日本膜鳴鼓，以鼓棒敲擊鼓面發聲。來源所見早期陶俑形象為肩掛桶形鼓，於腰高: Taiko is a Japanese membranophone, sounded by striking the head with sticks. The early clay figurines the source describes show a barrel drum hung from the shoulder and struck with sticks at hip height. A beginner can first master the basic rhythm, stance and grip, then practise dividing the work between the different drums; a kumidaiko ensemble usually pairs barrel-shaped nagado-daiko with the smaller shime-daiko. The drum music of noh differs in tempo, accent, force, pitch and function, and its rhythmic patterns are often strung together.
和太鼓音色渾厚有力，具有深沉而溫暖的質感。其音色明亮度取決於鼓皮張力與擊打方式，: Taiko has a deep, powerful timbre with a dark, warm quality. Its brightness depends on the tension of the head and the way it is struck, and it runs from a low muffled note to a crisp stroke. Its range is concentrated in the low and middle frequencies, where it can produce a stirring bass resonance. The way it resonates is unusual: the space inside the body amplifies the sound fully, for a penetrating effect. Beside a Western bass drum, taiko is more penetrating and warmer; beside an African drum its sound is heavier and has a traditional Eastern beauty. Its ability to be both forceful and delicate lets it play an important part in Japanese gagaku and in modern music alike.
